1.pericope_label: Then came certain of the elders of Israel unto me, and sat before me
debates: Whether the elders were exiles or a deputation from Jerusalem
What they came to the prophet for
Whether they were idolaters outright or only in disposition
outliers: Ellicott holds that no distinction is intended between the elders of Israel and the elders of Judah, so that no deputation need be supposed
Calvin reads the sitting as a posture of anxiety and despair, and takes the warning as a caution not to give way too easily when old men come to be disciples
Calvin finds an implied comparison, since God has set the seat of his empire in the heart and an idol there attempts to overthrow that throne
Keil and Delitzsch argue from the phrase itself that the elders were mentally busy with idols rather than given over to gross idolatry
themes: Idols carried where no image could be carried
A hope that a city would be spared for the sake of its few
The heart made an altar and a throne
Longing for what one dares not do

4.pericope_label: Therefore speak unto them, and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Every man of the house of Israel that setteth up his idols in his heart
debates: How an answer from God can itself be a judgment
What being taken in their own heart means
What the second verb of the call to repent governs
outliers: Ellicott states the principle that a man who persists against a known will is allowed to misunderstand it, instancing Balaam and Micaiah
Calvin distinguishes prophecy as an image of paternal care from an answer given as a judge, where no taste of favour can be perceived
Calvin rejects the readings that make the second verb mean wives or make yourselves return, and takes it of bringing others back with oneself
Calvin holds that where others wandered through our fault the injury must be made up by at least equal diligence
themes: An answer that seals a sentence already written
Flattery abandoned and the roaring that follows
A sword that makes some wise and stings others
Repentance proved by the hand stretched out to a brother

7.pericope_label: For every one of the house of Israel, or of the stranger that sojourneth in Israel, which separateth himself from me, and setteth up his idols in his heart
debates: Why the stranger is included in the threat
Whether the prophet consulted is a true or a false one
Whether the text or its margin should be followed in the last clause
outliers: Ellicott holds that the offence charged is not the idolatry itself but the attempt to join secret idolatry with inquiring of the Lord
Calvin turns the inclusion of the stranger into an aggravation, since a settler embracing the law did so accidentally while these were heirs by birth
Calvin observes that God never answers in himself without joining the effect to the prophecy, against men who call a threat thunder without lightning
Ellicott prefers the Hebrew text to the margin followed by the translators and the ancient versions, and would render it desolate for a sign
themes: A law that is one for the stranger and the home born
False prophets promising peace and believed for it
Setting the face as men do who engage hand to hand
A punishment that stands like a portent

9.pericope_label: And if the prophet be deceived when he hath spoken a thing, I the LORD have deceived that prophet
debates: In what sense God deceives a prophet
Whether the title prophet is granted to the deceiver
How destroying both parties can leave the covenant standing
outliers: Clarke states the rule that Hebrew says a thing is done by the Lord which he only permits, the government of God being so absolute that nothing occurs without his permission

Ellicott explains the deceiving as the working of ordained moral law, the same sense in which the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and adds that the man who refuses the medicine must sink under the disease
Calvin takes the title prophet as a concession of speech rather than a description, and admits the stumbling block it creates for the weak
Calvin answers the objection about the covenant by holding that the rigour itself is useful to the church, the obstinacy being otherwise incurable
themes: A shield made of more numerous flatterers
Bearing ones own sins with no surety to undertake
Sons made worse by indulgence
Righteous men present and a city not spared

12.pericope_label: The word of the LORD came again to me, saying, Son of man, when the land sinneth against me by trespassing grievously
debates: Whether a new prophecy begins here
What makes a land, rather than a man, a sinner
Where the sentence of the threat ends
outliers: Gill denies that a new prophecy begins here, taking it as the same word continued at the same time
Ellicott removes the definite article and turns the futures into presents, so that the verse reads as a standing rule rather than a description of one land
Henry explains the variety of judgments as a display of universal dominion, so that we may see our dependence in all our concerns
Calvin rejects the reading that ends the sentence at the stretching out of the hand, since the clause runs on into what follows
themes: Grievous sins bringing grievous plagues
A rod chosen by the one who wields it
No need of oppression where the staff of bread will do
Judgment that righteous men within will not turn aside

14.pericope_label: Though these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in it, they should deliver but their own souls by their righteousness, saith the Lord GOD
debates: Why these three names were chosen
Whether the Daniel meant is the contemporary or an older figure
How long the contemporary had been in exile
outliers: Ellicott holds the three were chosen as men allowed to be the means of saving others, and that Moses and Samuel were passed over because Jeremiah had used them
Ellicott finds the decisive propriety in Daniel being the trusted counsellor of the king by whom the city was to be destroyed
Clarke infers from the company that Job was as real a person as the other two, and reckons the exile at fourteen years against the twelve of Ellicott
Calvin denies that the parallel passage shows the dead interceding, since the construction is hypothetical throughout
themes: Men who had been the means of saving others
Righteousness that could not save a childs house
A captive among captives and a counsellor at court
Holiness that avails only for the man who has it

15.pericope_label: If I cause noisome beasts to pass through the land, and they spoil it, so that it be desolate, that no man may pass through because of the beasts
debates: Whether wild beasts act by chance or by command
How far the government of God reaches into a battle
Whether the rule laid down here always holds
outliers: Calvin argues that beasts would tear in pieces everyone they met unless held back by a secret instinct, so that letting them loose is as much an act as restraining them
Calvin claims that not only are the hands of men directed but their swords listen to a secret command, striking nothing except so far as God pleases
Calvin limits the doctrine, since God has manifold methods and no law can be imposed on him never to deliver anyone
Clarke explains the noisome beasts as multiplying in consequence of the general destruction of the inhabitants
themes: A scourge that Scripture names least often
An oath sworn by a life because there is no greater
Not one son or daughter saved by intercession
Four armies drawn up instead of one

22.pericope_label: Yet, behold, therein shall be left a remnant that shall be brought forth, both sons and daughters
debates: Whether the remnant is a mitigation of the judgment
In what sense the exiles are comforted
Whether the survivors bring repentance or only evidence
outliers: Calvin rejects the reading almost all give the verse, that God engages here to act more mercifully, and takes it instead as confirming the justice of the severity
Calvin argues that exile was worse than a single death, so that being brought out alive is no mitigation and those who died quickly were the less to be deplored
Ellicott holds that the phrase means the survivors will be a cause of comfort rather than administer it, and that by showing their exceeding wickedness
Calvin sets consolation against turbulent thoughts, holding that the mind is never tranquil until the equity of a judgment is present to it
themes: A remnant introduced with a note of admiration
Men dying daily rather than once
Comfort taken from the sight of wickedness
Justice without severity and mercy without caprice
